soil-agri-211.title: Cover crops as a shield against winter erosion
soil-agri-211.text: Winter and early spring leave many fields bare just when rain and wind erode them. Cover crops fill that gap. Their roots bind the soil, their residues maintain aggregation, and their leaves absorb raindrop energy, so less crusting occurs. They protect best when cut and mulched, or rolled and crimped, near maturity rather than worked in. At that stage they are somewhat lignified and their C:N ratios are not high enough to immobilize nutrients. Combined with mulching and no-till, they form conservation agriculture, which virtually eliminates runoff and erosion and has spread rapidly in temperate South America.

soil-agri-213.title: How organic materials hold soil in place
soil-agri-213.text: Organic matter works as a quiet erosion control. More soil organic matter gives better aggregation and less surface sealing, so more water infiltrates instead of running off and carrying soil away. Regular compost or manure additions stimulate earthworm activity and give larger, more stable aggregates. Where a farm uses zone-till or no-till, injecting manure limits disturbance, runoff and odor.

soil-agri-212.title: Sod in the rotation: perennial crops against erosion
soil-agri-212.text:
A sod crop in the rotation can cut erosion to a fraction. Washington research found winter wheat losing near 4 tons per acre a year with a sod crop in the rotation, versus about 15 tons without. Grass and legume forages keep a cover on most of the soil all year, and their roots hold it. Rotated with row crops, they keep erosion and runoff lower during the row-crop phase.

In strip cropping, strips of sod and row crop lie across the slope, so the sod filters erosion from the row crop. Each crop is grown two to five years on a strip, then rotated. Permanent sod as hay or pasture suits easily eroded steep soils, though slumping and landslides may concern on extremely steep slopes.

soil-agri-210.title: Surface residue cover and erosion
soil-agri-210.text: Cover on the surface decides how much soil leaves a field. Residues intercept raindrops and slow runoff. A moldboard plow may leave under 5% cover, chisel or disk systems over 30%, and continuous no-till 90% or more. Full cover virtually eliminates runoff and erosion on most agricultural land, and even 30% cover cuts erosion by 70%. Removing large amounts of residue permanently for fuel or building material harms soil health and resistance to erosion, especially when no manure is returned.

soil-agri-205.title: Why rare storms do most of the erosion damage
soil-agri-205.text: One storm can undo thirty years of care. About one-third of the water erosion damage in a field over 30 years commonly comes from a single extreme rainfall event. Wind works the same way: the 1930s Dust Bowl followed a decade of extremely dry years. Because such events are rare, the risk is easy to underestimate. Yet most erosion damage comes from them, and {{ref:soil-water-001}} is best judged by what the worst event can do.

soil-agri-221.title: Land use: what people do with a parcel
soil-agri-221.text:
Every parcel of land has a job. Land use describes what people do on it, covering the benefits taken from it and the management actions applied. The FAO defines it as the products and benefits obtained from land together with the management actions people carry out to obtain them. The IPCC defines it as the total of arrangements, activities and inputs applied to a parcel, and groups it into forest land, cropland, grassland, wetlands, settlements and other lands.

The choices matter for {{ref:soil-found-077}}, water, {{ref:soil-fert-181}}, plants and animals. Poor choices contribute to soil erosion, soil degradation, land degradation and desertification. Arable land was about 10.7% of the land surface in 2015, with 1.3% permanent cropland. Early-1990s figures were 13% arable, 26% pasture and 32% forest and woodland.

Governments plan and regulate land use through zoning and other ordinances to avoid land-use conflicts. An urban growth boundary is one such tool. The link to {{ref:soil-phys-246}} appears in the next entry, where land use changes.

soil-agri-222.title: Land use change and its carbon cost
soil-agri-222.text: Land use change is the shift from one {{ref:soil-agri-221}} category to another, mostly driven by human activity. With fossil fuel use, it is a major human source of carbon dioxide, a dominant {{ref:soil-phys-246}}. Deforestation, the permanent conversion of forest to other uses, has historically been a primary driver, and global forest cover has fallen by 35% since agriculture began. Urban areas cover just 3% of the Earth's surface, yet their growth shifts demand onto rural land and can take over adjacent cropland. Scientists track change with satellite and aircraft imagery, field observations and modelling, and use land change models to simulate futures for planning.

soil-agri-220.title: Soil phases: dividing a series by how it is used
soil-agri-220.text: A single soil series can behave very differently from one hillside to the next. Series vary so much in slope, erosion, stones or similar features that management advice could not be given if each were shown as one unit. So a {{ref:soil-class-037}} is divided into soil phases. The phase name gives the surface feature that most affects management. Vina loam 0 to 2 percent slopes and Vina gravelly loam 2 to 9 percent slopes are two of four phases of the Vina series. On a soil map, the area inside each continuous line is the delineation of a map unit, and a map unit includes the soil phase and all inclusions.

soil-agri-218.title: Reconnaissance surveys for poor land
soil-agri-218.text: Not every acre justifies a detailed survey. Large expanses with little direct agricultural or forest value are often too poor to repay the cost, so they are mapped at small scale. This is a reconnaissance soil survey. It shows regions dominated by soil associations rather than delineating individual soils, in contrast to the detailed map, where specific soils are outlined.

soil-agri-170.title: Web Soil Survey: soil maps on demand
soil-agri-170.text:
New surveys of the same county once took 30 to 60 years to appear. Web Soil Survey, run by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service, ended that wait. US surveys are no longer printed as books. They are published online, holding everything in the old county reports plus extra tools, and can be updated as needed. It gives access to data from the National Cooperative Soil Survey, building on the {{ref:soil-agri-082}} and the {{ref:soil-agri-084}}.

A user picks an area of interest anywhere in the United States where survey data exist. The Soil Map tab then shows the component soil map units, and a report can be saved as a PDF. The Soil Data Explorer gives properties for each map unit, such as depth to water table, surface texture, bulk density, pH and depth to a restrictive layer. It also gives suitability ratings, with reasons, for uses such as dwellings with basements, local roads and streets, vegetative productivity and wastewater disposal by irrigation. It is one recognized basis, alongside measured infiltration rates, for choosing the hydrologic soil group of a site.

soil-meth-058.title: Soil test calibration: what a number really means
soil-meth-058.text:
A soil test number means nothing until someone matches it to a harvest. That multi-year matching is soil test calibration. Researchers apply different nutrient levels, always including zero, to plots on many fields over several years, and compare yields. A new test cannot be called useful until it has been correlated with plant response on varied soils and weather, and small-plot results must be validated on commercial farms.

Calibration matters because a {{ref:soil-fert-187}} estimates a few nutrients from a small sample meant to represent many acres, so it is not 100% accurate. A low test may fail to raise yield if it is poorly calibrated for that soil, or if drainage or compaction harms the crop. Extra nutrients on a high-testing soil occasionally help when weather reduces availability.

soil-meth-057.title: Taking a soil sample that represents the field
soil-meth-057.text:
A lab can only be as right as the sample it receives. Soil sampling for fertility testing collects a representative composite of cores from a field. Samples are usually taken in fall or spring before the season and analysed for pH, lime requirement, P, K, Ca and Mg. Repeat at the same season and with the same lab so that years are comparable.

Take cores from at least 15-20 random spots per field or zone, whatever its size. One sample should represent no more than 10-20 acres, or 1-5 acres for precision zone or grid management. Sample between rows, avoid old fence rows and dead furrows, and sample problem areas separately, since nutrient levels vary with crop history and topography.

Depth depends on the field. Sample cultivated fields to plow depth and permanent pasture to 3 or 4 inches. Sample no-till fields twice: 6 inches for lime and fertilizer advice and 2 inches to monitor surface acidity. Mix the cores in a clean container, remove roots and stones and air dry. Sample fields at least every three years. The result feeds a {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-059.title: Which phosphorus test? It depends on the region
soil-meth-059.text:
No single test measures plant-available phosphorus everywhere. The extractant varies by region: Olsen and AB-DTPA in arid and semiarid western areas, Mehlich 3 or Bray 1 in the humid Midwest and East, Mehlich 1 in the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, and Morgan in the Northeast. In Washington and Oregon, Bray 1 is used for acidic soils and Olsen for alkaline soils. These are regional chemical extractions, each with its own numeric range.

Optimum ranges in ppm P are Olsen 11-16, Bray 1 25-45, Mehlich 1 20-40 and Mehlich 3 30-50. In calcareous soil the Olsen optimum is higher, with over 25 ppm for zero P fertilizer. A soil high in P by one test is generally high by another, though the numbers differ. Low and medium levels mean likely yield gain from P, while high levels raise the potential for P pollution in runoff. Tests capture P from recent manure and from soil minerals, but active organic matter from residues or manure may supply more than the test shows. All of this builds on the {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-056.title: Sample preparation before the instrument
soil-meth-056.text: Instruments rarely measure soil as it comes from the field. Sample preparation is the treatment a sample receives so it is in a form the instrument can measure. It matters because techniques are often unresponsive to the analyte in its in-situ form, or results are distorted by interfering species. Steps can include crushing and dissolution, acid or alkali digestion, extraction, clean-up and pre-concentration. They may also involve pulverizing, filtering, dilution, masking, sub-sampling or treatment with a chelating agent such as EDTA.

soil-meth-055.title: Certified reference materials: a lab's yardstick
soil-meth-055.text:
Most analytical instruments are comparative: they only say how a sample differs from something known. So labs need controls or standards of known composition, used to check quality and traceability, validate methods and calibrate instruments. A certified reference material differs from a laboratory reagent in its certificate, which gives the value, its uncertainty and a statement of metrological traceability.

Accreditation under ISO/IEC 17025 requires traceability to such materials where possible, and prefers them where available. ILAC lists five types: pure substances, standard solutions and gas mixtures, matrix materials, physico-chemical materials, and reference objects. Natural matrix materials are made by homogenizing a natural sample to a fine powder, since natural materials are rarely homogeneous at the gram scale, then measuring each analyte. Producers test homogeneity on 10-30 randomly chosen units with two or three subsamples each, and test stability by real-time or accelerated storage studies.

soil-meth-062.title: From test value to advice: the interpretation categories
soil-meth-062.text: A lab report turns a number into a verdict. Labs sort each value into categories, tied to the probability that adding the nutrient will raise yield, as set by {{ref:soil-meth-058}}. The categories run very low, low, optimum, high and excessive, with probability of response falling from very high to very low. For the pre-sidedress nitrate test on corn 6-12 inches tall sampled to 1 foot, nitrate-N of 11-22 ppm is low, 23-28 optimum and over 35 excessive. Ranges depend on the extractant: for Mehlich 3 in North Carolina, P is optimum at 26-50 ppm. Reports adapt advice using the manure and previous crop information supplied, but legume cover crop N is usually not credited, and manure decided on later is missed.

soil-meth-061.title: Reading odd soil test results
soil-meth-061.text:
Strange numbers usually have a history behind them. Very high phosphorus comes from years of heavy poultry or other manure. Very high pH with high calcium relative to K and Mg points to lime-stabilized sewage sludge. High salt in humid regions can come from large poultry manure doses in high tunnels, where rain cannot leach salts, or from deicing salt beside a road.

The other cause is the wrong extractant. Acid extractants (Morgan, Mehlich 1 or 3) dissolve free limestone and give too much calcium. On alkaline calcareous soils (pH above 7) they extract little P because the soil neutralizes the acid. Many labs also report the CEC the soil would have at pH 7 or higher, whereas the textbook estimates current CEC by summing the exchangeable bases.

soil-meth-060.title: Sensing a crop's nitrogen from the field to orbit
soil-meth-060.text:
Crop nitrogen sensing assesses a crop's nitrogen status in season, to guide fertilizer rates, and extends the {{ref:soil-fert-195}}. Chlorophyll meters estimate leaf chlorophyll as an N indicator. They need field visits and adequate leaf sampling and are mainly used for final cereal applications. Canopy reflectance sensors read near-infrared and red or red-edge light. Mounted on equipment, they adjust N on the go, usually with a high-N reference strip for calibration.

Satellite, aircraft or drone imagery uses the same bands at 10-30 m resolution. Satellites are limited by cloud cover, and aircraft and drones are more expensive. Computer models simulate field N dynamics daily and are cheap and scalable, but involve no direct field observation.

soil-fert-188.title: Grid sampling for site-specific rates
soil-fert-188.text: Grid soil sampling splits a large field into points and analyses each separately, to guide site-specific nutrient and lime rates. The general recommendation is 2.5- to 5-acre grids, especially where manure and fertilizer rates varied; some areas use one-acre grids. Unaligned grids are advised: points are shifted randomly off the regular grid so that a past applicator malfunction is not unknowingly sampled in a line. Each point still needs 10-15 cores within about 30 feet. Because grid testing is expensive, do it once per rotation, when lime may be needed, or every five to eight years. Fertility patterns often do not follow soil survey maps, which is why the grid earns its cost. It extends the basic {{ref:soil-fert-187}}.

soil-meth-063.title: Testing the soil in a high tunnel
soil-meth-063.text: A tomato crop in a high tunnel eats far more than a field crop. Tunnel tomatoes reaching the equivalent of 60-80 tons per acre need roughly 200-300 lb N, 300-400 lb P2O5 and 700-900 lb K2O per acre. Rain does not leach salts there, so they build up. Recommendations from routine field soil tests must be adjusted upward. A saturated media extract measures water-soluble nutrients, including nitrate-N and ammonium-N, plus total salinity.
